Below are two statements, I and II. They may be independent causes, effects of independent causes, or effects of a common cause; one may also be the cause of the other. Read both statements and decide how they are related.

I. The banking regulator required every lender to show borrowers, before a small loan is signed, one all-inclusive annual cost figure covering interest, fees and insurance.
II. In the months that followed, several microfinance lenders that had advertised low interest rates but charged heavy fees lost many borrowers to banks.
options: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both the statements I and II are independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

steps: Once all costs appear in one figure, borrowers can see that the "cheap" loans are in fact costly, and they move to banks. "In the months that followed" places II after I. I is the cause and II its effect.
solution.trap: It is tempting to read II as the reason for the rule (regulators act on mis-selling), but II reports borrowers leaving after the rule; it is the rule's result.

I. The state has stopped issuing licences for new borewells in 40 of its blocks.
II. For a decade, the groundwater table in those 40 blocks has fallen by more than a metre every year.
options: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both the statements I and II are independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

steps: A decade of falling water tables (II) led the state to stop new borewells in exactly those blocks (I). II is the cause and I is its effect.
solution.trap: "Common cause: over-extraction" is tempting, but II is the measured decline itself, and I is the response to it; nothing more is needed.

items.prompt:
Below are two statements, I and II. They may be independent causes, effects of independent causes, or effects of a common cause; one may also be the cause of the other. Read both statements and decide how they are related.

I. Malaria cases in the district fell sharply this year after insecticide-treated bed nets were given to every household.
II. The number of tuberculosis cases detected in the district rose this year after mobile X-ray vans began screening villagers.
options: Statement I is the cause and statement II is its effect
Statement II is the cause and statement I is its effect
Both the statements I and II are independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of independent causes
Both the statements I and II are effects of some common cause

steps: Each statement gives its own cause: bed nets for I, screening vans for II.
II reports more cases detected, the result of better screening, not of worsening health; the two causes are unrelated, so the statements are effects of independent causes.
solution.trap: "Malaria down, TB up" looks like a contrast that needs one explanation, but each figure has its own stated cause and neither affects the other.
